world_behind.title: The second reading: Isaiah 49
world_behind.text: Where chapter 20 scolded and promised, this text turns to the Servant: called from the womb, hidden like a weapon, despairing of his labor, and given as "a light to the Gentiles" (v. 6). The reading also carries the fullest scattering-and-gathering promises Nephi has. His interpretation in chapter 22 will spend itself on them.

world_behind.title: The Servant's double identity
world_behind.text: The figure is addressed as "my servant, O Israel" (v. 3) yet labors to "bring Jacob again to him" (v. 5): Israel personified, and a person sent to Israel, in the same poem. The ambiguity is ancient and productive; the record will read the Servant both ways, nation and Messiah, without forcing a choice.

world_behind.title: A weapons cache of words
world_behind.text: "A sharp sword" (v. 2), "a polished shaft" (v. 2), hidden in hand and quiver: the Servant is armament kept concealed until needed. Polishing a shaft is fletcher's work, slow abrasion toward flight; the figure gives the delay itself a purpose, which a family twenty years into a detour could hear.

world_behind.title: Engraved palms
world_behind.text: "I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands" (v. 16) answers Zion's complaint with the era's most permanent writing technology, the same verb this record uses for its own plates. A name written on skin wears off; one graven cannot. The verse puts Zion where a workman cannot look without seeing her.

world_behind.title: Nursing kings
world_behind.text: "Kings shall be thy nursing fathers" (v. 23) inverts the ancient order: monarchs who took tribute and children now carry the children home and feed them. Court prostration ( "lick up the dust of thy feet" (v. 23)) is aimed at Zion by her former masters: the exiles' humiliations run backward.

world_behind.title: Sinim and the compass points
world_behind.text: The gathered come from north, west, and "the land of Sinim" (v. 12), a place-name so far its location was already obscure: the point is horizon-breaking distance. For hearers who themselves came by sea to a land off every map, the roll call of far places includes, implicitly, theirs.

words.text: Not preachers in the modern sense. A pastor is a shepherd, and Jeremiah, who prophesied in the Jerusalem Lehi left, aimed the word at leaders who scattered their own flock (Jer. 23:1). The preface added to this chapter uses his idiom to explain the scattering it addresses, "the wickedness of the pastors of my people" (v. 1), and that is the single time the word appears in the volume. Blame is assigned to the shepherds before anything at all is said about the sheep.

words.text: "Made me a polished shaft" (v. 2): an arrow worked smooth so it flies true, then hidden "in his quiver" (v. 2). The verb costs time and friction, and the hiddenness is storage. The Servant's obscurity, and every believer's, is here a weapon's waiting.

words.text: Not acceptable in the sense of adequate. The time is acceptable because God accepts it, a window opened on his clock: "In an acceptable time have I heard thee" (v. 8), matched with "a day of salvation" (v. 8). Paul lifts the pair to insist the window is open at the moment of speaking (2 Cor. 6:2). Nothing in the verse makes the hearing wait on the exile getting ready to be heard.

words.text: Inherited holdings, land that came to a family by descent. The plural appears once in this record and once in the King James Bible, and both are this same verse of Isaiah. The servant is given "to cause to inherit the desolate heritages" (v. 8), which names a specific job: restoring land somebody already owned and lost.

words.text: The word is narrow, whatever its sound suggests to a modern ear. Children born after the loss press in until "The place is too strait for me" (v. 20), a complaint about floor space from a woman who was childless a few verses earlier. Elsewhere the record keeps the adjective for its path (1 Ne. 8:20), where narrowness is a limit. Here it is the evidence that the gathering worked.

The next verse answers with the chapter's boldest mechanics: the Lord contends with the contender, and the meal is taken back out of the predator's mouth.

phrases.term: All ye that are broken off
phrases.text: The block's largest variant: before the KJV's opening ("Listen, O isles, unto me," Isa. 49:1), the record carries a full verse addressing "all ye that are broken off and are driven out" (v. 1), scattered "because of the wickedness of the pastors of my people" (v. 1). The added preface aims the whole poem at exactly the audience Nephi named at 19:24, a broken-off branch, before the first KJV word arrives.

phrases.text: Where the KJV reads only "and in a day of salvation have I helped thee" (Isa. 49:8), the record inserts the address "O isles of the sea" (v. 8), and later "my servant" (v. 8) for the covenant-giving. The isles, Zenos's word for the scattered (19:16), are written into the poem's second-person: the far branches are not eavesdropping on Israel's mail; they are named in it.

phrases.text: The KJV's burst of praise ("Sing, O heavens; and be joyful, O earth; and break forth into singing, O mountains," Isa. 49:13) gains two clauses: "the feet of those who are in the east shall be established" (v. 13) and "for they shall be smitten no more" (v. 13). The variant adds standing ground and an end of striking to the singing: comfort with substance in it for people mid-scattering.

phrases.text: The answer to forgottenness is engraving, this record's own verb for permanence: what is cut into metal, or flesh, outlasts every lapse of attention. Zion is remembered the way a scar is carried, and the walls of the ruined city stand "continually before me" (v. 16).

phrases.term: I will lift up mine hand to the Gentiles
phrases.text: The gathering's mechanism: a signal ("my standard to the people" (v. 22)), then foreign arms carrying "thy sons" (v. 22) and "thy daughters" (v. 22) home. Jacob will requote this passage almost immediately (2 Ne. 6:6) and Nephi will interpret it in the next chapter: of everything in the reading, this is the verse the small plates cannot leave alone.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: The chapter opens with a sentence Isaiah 49 does not have
verses.text: Set against the King James text, eighteen of these twenty-six verses differ in wording, and the largest difference is here at the start: some forty words of address prefixed before the servant speaks, naming the hearers and their condition and calling them the house of Israel twice over. Isaiah 49 begins with the isles. The record begins by telling a scattered people that it is the one being spoken to.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: The one substantive cut in the chapter
verses.text: Almost every variant in these verses adds something. Verse 7 removes: the King James clause naming the Holy One of Israel choosing the servant is not here, and nation becomes nations. The record does not trim this text anywhere else, which is what makes the one place it does worth marking.

verses.label: v. 8–9
verses.title: An address added, and a state turned into a posture
verses.text: Verse 8 gains a vocative and a title that the King James verse does not carry. Verse 9 makes a smaller change with more in it: those who are in darkness become those who sit in darkness. A condition becomes a position, which is something a person can be told to get up from.

verses.label: v. 12–13
verses.title: The additions promise that the striking stops
verses.text: Verse 12 gains a direct address to the house of Israel. Verse 13 gains two whole clauses the King James text lacks, one establishing the feet of those in the east and one promising they shall be smitten no more. Isaiah's verse ends in comfort and mercy; the record ends this one on a guarantee about the future.

verses.label: v. 14–15
verses.title: The complaint is answered inside its own verse
verses.text: In Isaiah, Zion's charge that the Lord has forsaken and forgotten her stands alone, and the reply arrives in the verse after. Here a clause is appended to the charge itself, so the accusation and its denial share one sentence. Verse 15 then adds another address to the house of Israel, the third such insertion in the chapter.

verses.label: v. 20
verses.title: One word changes the arithmetic of the promise
verses.text: The King James verse has the children thou shalt have "after thou hast lost the other." This version reads the first. The children are no longer a different set from some other set; they are the ones who come after a first loss, which makes the verse a sequence rather than a substitution.

verses.label: v. 24–26
verses.title: The alterations thin out before the end
verses.text: Across the last three verses the differences from the King James text are down to spelling and a stray conjunction: captive for captives, savior for saviour, one dropped and. A chapter that opened with forty added words closes in near-agreement with the text it is quoting.

chapter.title: The text answers its introduction
chapter.text: Nephi promised hope for "all ye that are broken off" (v. 1) at 19:24, and this block's opening variant addresses precisely that congregation before Isaiah's first word. Reading and audience interlock so tightly that the likening method looks less like application than like delivery of addressed mail.

spans.text: all ye that are broken off

chapter.title: A Servant for the despairing servant
chapter.text: The poem's center is a called man who thinks he has failed and is answered with a larger commission. Nephi, whose workings in the spirit weary his joints (19:20) and whose own mission to his brothers keeps failing, reads aloud a text in which vain labor is a stage of the call.

chapter.title: The variants aim the poem outward
chapter.text: Each major divergence (the broken-off preface, the isles-of-the-sea address, the established feet in the east, the he-will-show assurance) widens the audience or firms the promise. As in chapter 20, the brass-plates text is the more explicit reading, and its explicitness runs toward the scattered.

chapter.title: Forgottenness is met with anatomy
chapter.text: The complaint at verse 14 is quoted before it is answered, "The Lord hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me," and the reply is anatomical rather than argumentative. Verse 15 offers a nursing mother and grants that even she may fail, "they may forget, yet will I not forget thee." Verse 16 moves the evidence onto a body, "I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands." Two verses, two body parts, and no appeal to memory at all.

chapter.title: The gathering has logistics
chapter.text: Standard, signal, carrying arms, nursing kings, contested prey: this is not vague hope but mechanism, and it is why chapter 22 exists. Nephi's brothers ask their first real doctrinal question because this chapter's promises are concrete enough to argue about.

chapter.title: Reversal is the poem's grammar
chapter.text: Five reversals are stated in the chapter and each names both states. Verse 7 has "him whom man despiseth" become one before whom "kings shall see and arise." Verse 9 has prisoners told "Go forth" and given pastures. Verses 20 and 21 have the bereaved say "The place is too strait for me." Verse 25 has "the prey of the terrible" delivered. Verse 26 has the oppressors "drunken with their own blood." Every station of the exile is run backward, and the last of the five turns the oppressor into his own victim.

chapter.title: The unit's hinge to interpretation
chapter.text: Two chapters of assigned reading end with the strongest possible claims about the isles and the Gentiles, and no application sentence. Chapter 22 opens with the brothers asking whether all this is spiritual or temporal: the reading has done its work, and the discussion can begin.

applications.title: Read your obscurity as a quiver
applications.text: If your gifts feel hidden, ask whether they are being stored rather than shelved: polished, protected, and dated for a flight not yet called. Keep sharpening in the dark; concealment in this poem is custody.

applications.title: Answer despair with assignment
applications.text: When labor feels spent for naught, notice the poem's therapy: the Servant's cure was a bigger errand. Rest was never on offer. Take on the small next assignment (a person, a class, a calling) and let enlargement do what consolation cannot.

applications.title: Keep a graven list
applications.text: Write the names you are tempted to believe God has forgotten, your own included, and read them against the palms verse. Then practice the divine method on your own scale: put the people you must not forget where your work forces you to see them.

applications.title: Audit your complaint
applications.text: Zion's "the Lord hath forsaken me" was answerable, and the record's variant says so immediately. State your own version of the complaint out loud, then list the demonstrations already on record. Most forsakenness dissolves under inventory.

applications.title: Carry someone's children
applications.text: In the gathering, outsiders do the carrying. Find one practical way this season to be the Gentile arms of the promise: transport, meals, tuition, testimony, whatever brings someone's sons and daughters nearer home.

applications.title: Wait without shame
applications.text: The verse's last clause is the whole program: "they shall not be ashamed that wait for me" (v. 23). Name the promise you are tired of waiting on, and retire the embarrassment of still believing it; in this chapter the waiters are the ones vindicated.

questions.text: What has the delay in my life polished that immediate use would have left rough?
When I last said "I have labored in vain," what did I do with the feeling, and what does the Servant's example suggest?
Whose forgetting do I actually fear, God's or people's, and does my prayer life know the difference?
What would change today if I believed my name were engraved where God cannot avoid seeing it?
Where has God's arithmetic already outrun mine: what do I have that I never begot and cannot account for?
Which "mighty" currently holds something of mine, and do I believe the promise in verse 25 applies to it?
